title: D & G Stout, Inc. v. Bacardi Imports, Inc.
summary: A supplier’s assurance that it would keep an at-will distributorship cannot support recovery of future profits, but it can support reliance damages for a priced sale opportunity the distributor gave up on the strength of the assurance; the Seventh Circuit sent the case to trial, where the distributor recovered $394,050 plus interest.
notes:
Court: Seventh Circuit (1991), applying Indiana law.

923 F.2d 566 (7th Cir. 1991), decided January 31, 1991. After Bacardi withdrew, National's renewed offer was $550,000 lower than its earlier one; the court allowed recovery of that differential as reliance loss but not lost profits, because an at-will promise cannot be reasonably relied on for future profits.

sections.Parties: D & G Stout, Inc., successor to General Liquors, Inc., the operating distributor the opinions call General, was the plaintiff and appellant. Bacardi Imports, Inc., a major liquor supplier that used General as its northern Indiana wholesale distributor, was the defendant and appellee. National Wine & Spirits Company, a competing distributor, offered to buy General’s assets; Hiram Walker, another supplier, later withdrew its line.
sections.Material Facts: General, based in South Bend, had distributed Bacardi products in northern Indiana at will for more than thirty-five years. In spring 1987 two major suppliers withdrew their lines, and General’s president, David Stout, concluded it could stay profitable if it kept Bacardi, Hiram Walker and Canandaigua. On July 9 National’s James LaCrosse approached Stout about buying General, and at a Bacardi meeting in Indianapolis that day Stout disclosed the contemplated sale and sought a commitment; Bacardi emphatically said it intended to stay. General and National negotiated an asset sale over two weeks. By July 22–23 the financial terms were settled; Stout again sought assurances, Bacardi unequivocally recommitted, and General rejected National’s offer on July 23. That afternoon Bacardi decided to move its line and told General on July 30. General sold to National on August 28 at a price it said was $550,000 below the July proposal.
sections.Procedural History: D & G Stout sued Bacardi in the Northern District of Indiana under diversity jurisdiction for the decline in the business’s sale value on a promissory-estoppel theory. Judge Robert L. Miller, Jr. granted Bacardi summary judgment, treating an open-ended at-will assurance as one Indiana law would not let General rely on. The Seventh Circuit (Cudahy, J., with Posner and Flaum, JJ.) reversed on January 31, 1991, 923 F.2d 566, and remanded for trial. After a bench trial the district court found the promise conditional on market and performance conditions and Bacardi unaware of the National negotiations, but found every element of promissory estoppel under an objective foreseeability standard and awarded $394,050 in reliance damages plus $116,400 in prejudgment interest, 805 F. Supp. 1434 (1992).
sections.Issue: At summary judgment, did Indiana promissory-estoppel law permit General to seek the value of a known sale opportunity it allegedly surrendered in reasonable reliance on Bacardi’s assurance of a continuing at-will distributorship, or did the at-will nature of the relationship make such reliance unreasonable and the claimed loss an impermissible demand for future profits?
sections.Holding: The claim could proceed. Because the assurance fixed no term, General could not recover expected future profits from Bacardi sales, but it could recover reliance damages for the existing National opportunity it allegedly gave up. Bacardi knew General was deciding whether to sell, repeatedly encouraged it to continue, and could foresee an immediate loss of bargaining position if it withdrew. Summary judgment was reversed and the case remanded for proof of the promise, reliance, causation and damages.
sections.Reasoning: Indiana’s § 90 rule binds a promise that foreseeably induces action or forbearance when enforcement is needed to avoid injustice, with relief calibrated to justice. The court drew an analogy to an indefinite at-will job offer: it supplies no fixed future wage because discharge can follow hiring immediately, yet Indiana cases protect reliance costs such as moving expenses and wages forgone in preparing for the job. General sought the value of a priced July sale it surrendered by choosing to continue, and Bacardi’s withdrawal then destroyed that alternative and General’s leverage. National already carried a competing rum and never expected to keep the Bacardi account, so the price drop measured the loss of General’s independent-operation alternative rather than the capitalized value of Bacardi profits. The later trial refined the picture: the promise was conditional and Bacardi lacked actual knowledge of the National talks, but it knew its line was essential to General’s survival and should have expected General to forgo exit opportunities; comparing the rejected July terms with the August recoveries, the court awarded $510,450 in all.

priorVersions.summary: An at-will distributorship could generate a recoverable reliance loss when repeated assurances induced rejection of a concrete sale opportunity.
priorVersions.notes:
Court: Seventh Circuit (1991), applying Indiana law.

Keep the appeal and the editors’ outcome-on-remand note separate. The book reports a $550,000 alleged differential on appeal and a $394,050 later award; neither number should replace the other. The later trial found conditions concerning sales expectations and market changes. The court did not decide a universal time during which reliance on an at-will assurance remains reasonable.

sections.Parties: D & G Stout, successor to General Liquors, sued Bacardi, a major supplier in its Northern Indiana distribution business.
sections.Material Facts: General had lost suppliers and was choosing between remaining independent and selling its assets to National. Bacardi repeatedly assured General that it would continue their relationship while knowing of the sale negotiations. General rejected the negotiated offer. Bacardi decided to withdraw its account that same afternoon and communicated the withdrawal later. General’s bargaining leverage collapsed, and it alleged a sale-price reduction of $550,000.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment for Bacardi because the relationship remained terminable at will. The Seventh Circuit reversed and remanded for trial, treating General’s allegations as still needing proof. A separate casebook note reports that the trial court later found a conditional commitment and awarded $394,050 in reliance damages.
sections.Issue: Did the at-will nature of the relationship make all reliance unreasonable, and was the price reduction a lost-profit expectancy or a loss from an opportunity forgone?
sections.Holding: The alleged reliance injury could be actionable despite the at-will relationship. The appellate decision allowed a trial; it did not award the alleged $550,000 or create a permanent distributorship.
sections.Reasoning: The buyer of General’s assets did not expect to acquire Bacardi’s account. The lower price therefore could represent the loss of General’s ability to reject a liquidation offer, rather than the capitalized value of future Bacardi profits. The opinion analogizes this to moving costs or wages forgone in preparing for promised at-will employment, distinguishing them from wages expected from the new job. Reasonableness and the actual terms and duration of the assurance remained matters for trial.

learning.why: The useful distinction is between an uncertain future benefit and a concrete opportunity surrendered because of an assurance. “At will” does not answer both questions by itself.

topics.promissory-estoppel: A specific assurance can have legal consequences despite an at-will relationship.
topics.reliance-damages: The alleged injury was a foregone sale opportunity and lost bargaining leverage.
topics.expectation: Future distributorship profits were distinguished from the loss claimed.
topics.precontractual-liability: Reliance during a business decision may cause loss before a new long-term bargain exists.
topics.at-will-reliance: The case is the leading treatment of reliance on assurances within a terminable-at-will relationship.
topics.reliance-interest: Recovery was limited to the forgone sale price differential, a reliance measure, not lost distributorship profits.
topics.promise-or-prediction: The court asked whether Bacardi's statements were reasonably understood as a commitment rather than a mere expression of present intention.
